definition: Running one or more complete guest operating systems on a single physical computer, each inside its own virtual machine, with a hypervisor sharing out the real CPU, memory and devices.
example: One 64-core server can run thirty virtual machines, each booting its own Linux or Windows kernel.

definition: Another name for a hypervisor: the software that creates virtual machines and keeps control of the real hardware. With KVM the word often means the userspace program (QEMU, Firecracker) that emulates devices, while KVM handles the CPU side.
example: Firecracker is a VMM: a userspace process that asks KVM to run guest vCPUs and emulates a few virtio devices.

definition: The operating system running inside a virtual machine. It believes it controls the hardware, but the hypervisor decides what it really gets.
example: Ubuntu running inside VirtualBox on a Windows laptop is the guest OS; Windows is the host.

definition: The operating system that runs directly on the physical machine and hosts virtual machines or containers. For native containers it is the one kernel every container shares.
example: Containers on a Linux server all make their system calls into the same host kernel.

definition: Moving several lightly loaded physical servers onto one host as virtual machines, to save hardware, power and space.
example: Ten servers each using 5% of their CPU can often be consolidated as VMs onto one or two hosts.

definition: A hypervisor that runs directly on the hardware, with no general-purpose operating system underneath it. Used for servers and clouds.
example: VMware ESXi, Xen and Hyper-V are type 1 hypervisors; KVM is usually classed as one too.

definition: A hypervisor that runs as an application on top of an ordinary host operating system and relies on it for scheduling, memory and drivers. Common on desktops.
example: VirtualBox installed on a Windows laptop is a type 2 hypervisor.

definition: A Linux kernel module that turns Linux into a hypervisor by driving the CPU's hardware virtualisation (VT-x or AMD-V). A userspace VMM such as QEMU or Firecracker runs each VM as a process with one thread per vCPU.
example: QEMU calls the KVM_RUN ioctl on a vCPU thread; KVM runs the guest until a VM exit needs attention.

definition: Microsoft's type 1 hypervisor. Once enabled it runs underneath Windows, which itself becomes a privileged guest (the root partition).
example: Enabling WSL 2 on Windows turns on parts of Hyper-V.

definition: VMware's type 1 hypervisor for servers. It boots directly on the hardware rather than running inside another operating system.
An open-source type 1 hypervisor from the University of Cambridge (2003). It introduced paravirtualisation on x86, where guest kernels are modified to make hypercalls.
example: Early Amazon EC2 instances ran on Xen.

definition: A free type 2 hypervisor from Oracle that runs as an application on Windows, macOS or Linux.
VMware's type 2 (hosted) hypervisor for desktop computers.
A type 2 hypervisor for macOS, commonly used to run Windows on a Mac.
An open-source x86 emulator that interprets every guest instruction in software instead of running it directly on the CPU. Portable and precise, but much slower than virtualisation.

An open-source machine emulator and userspace VMM. With KVM it runs guest code on the real CPU and emulates devices such as disks and network cards; without KVM it can translate other CPU architectures in software.
example: QEMU can pretend to be an Intel e1000 network card so an unmodified guest driver works.

definition: A userspace VMM written in Rust by Google, used for running VMs on ChromeOS on top of KVM.
An open-source userspace VMM written in Rust that runs on KVM (and Microsoft's MSHV), aimed at modern cloud workloads with a small device model.
A piece of code loaded into the running Linux kernel, such as a driver or KVM. Loading one needs CAP_SYS_MODULE in the initial user namespace, because module code runs with full kernel privilege.
example: modprobe kvm_intel loads the KVM module for Intel CPUs.

definition: Everything that runs outside the kernel, in the CPU's less privileged mode: ordinary programs, daemons and libraries. They reach the kernel only through system calls.
example: QEMU runs in userspace; KVM runs in the kernel.

definition: A CPU as seen by a guest. The hypervisor schedules each vCPU onto real CPU cores; with KVM each vCPU is a host thread.
example: A VM with 4 vCPUs shows four processors to the guest, but they may share fewer physical cores.

definition: The classic way to virtualise a CPU: run the guest kernel with reduced privilege so that ordinary instructions run directly, while privileged ones trap to the hypervisor, which emulates their effect on the guest's virtual state.
example: When a deprivileged guest runs cli, the CPU traps; the hypervisor records 'interrupts off' for that vCPU and resumes the guest.

definition: A synchronous transfer of control from running code to more privileged software (the kernel or hypervisor), triggered by the instruction itself, for example a privileged instruction run in user mode.
Running code at a lower privilege level than it was written for, such as running a guest kernel in user mode, so its privileged instructions trap to the hypervisor.

Software that reproduces the behaviour of hardware (a CPU, or a device such as a network card) so code written for that hardware runs unchanged. Faithful, but every emulated operation costs software work.
example: QEMU emulating an e1000 network card handles each register access the guest driver makes.

definition: Executing a program by decoding and simulating each machine instruction in software, rather than letting the real CPU run it.
An instruction the CPU only allows in its most privileged mode (kernel mode, ring 0). Run anywhere else it causes a trap.
example: Loading the page-table base (CR3) and halting the CPU (HLT) are privileged on x86.

definition: In Popek and Goldberg's model, an instruction that changes the machine's configuration (control-sensitive) or whose result depends on the mode or location it runs in (behaviour-sensitive). The hypervisor must see every one.
example: x86 POPF is sensitive but not privileged, so it does not trap in user mode.

definition: Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg's 1974 conditions for virtualisation: equivalence, resource control and efficiency. Their theorem says a machine can be virtualised by trap-and-emulate if every sensitive instruction is privileged.
example: Classic x86 failed the test because about 17 sensitive instructions did not trap.

definition: Popek–Goldberg property: a program behaves the same in a virtual machine as on real hardware, apart from timing and resource availability.
Popek–Goldberg property: the VMM keeps complete control of the real resources, so a guest cannot use memory or devices it was not given.
Popek–Goldberg property: the vast majority of guest instructions run directly on the hardware without the VMM stepping in.

A condition that guarantees a result when it holds, without being the only way to get that result. Popek–Goldberg's condition guarantees virtualisability, but a CPU failing it can still be virtualised by other means such as binary translation.
The x86 instruction that pops a value from the stack into the flags register. In user mode it silently leaves the interrupt flag unchanged instead of trapping, which broke classic trap-and-emulate.
A bit in the x86 flags register that says whether the CPU accepts maskable hardware interrupts. A hypervisor keeps a virtual copy per vCPU instead of letting guests change the real one.

The x86 instructions that clear (cli) and set (sti) the interrupt flag, disabling or enabling maskable interrupts. They fault when the current privilege level is above IOPL, so a deprivileged guest kernel traps when it runs them.
The x86 ring the CPU is currently executing in, from 0 (most privileged, the kernel) to 3 (user programs).
A two-bit field in the x86 flags register. Code whose CPL is greater than IOPL may not change the interrupt flag or use I/O ports directly.
The x86 operating mode, introduced with the 80286 and 80386, that provides privilege rings, segmentation and paging. Modern 64-bit long mode builds on it.
An old x86 mode for running 16-bit real-mode programs inside protected mode, with its own special rules for flag and interrupt instructions.
x86 instructions that store the location of the global and interrupt descriptor tables. They do not trap in user mode, so a guest could see where the real tables are and detect the hypervisor.
In-memory tables the x86 CPU uses to describe memory segments (the global descriptor table, GDT) and interrupt handlers (the interrupt descriptor table, IDT).
One of the x86 CPU's privilege levels, numbered 0 (most privileged, where the kernel runs) to 3 (least privileged, where applications run).
example: Linux uses ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for processes; rings 1 and 2 are normally unused.

definition: The CPU's privileged mode, in which privileged instructions are allowed and all memory can be reached. The kernel (or hypervisor) runs here.
The CPU's restricted mode for ordinary programs. Privileged instructions trap, and only memory the kernel has mapped is reachable.
Rewriting machine code into different machine code just before it runs. VMware used it to replace a guest kernel's problem instructions, such as POPF, with safe sequences.
The memory where a binary translator keeps blocks it has already rewritten, so hot code is translated once and reused.
A straight-line run of instructions with one entry at the top and one exit at the bottom, with no jumps in or out in the middle. Translators and compilers work a block at a time.
Code that writes over its own instructions while running. A binary translator must notice and retranslate it.
An exception reported so that every earlier instruction has finished and no later one has had any effect, making the exact faulting instruction identifiable.
A jump whose target address comes from a register or memory at run time, so a translator cannot know it in advance.
Modifying the guest kernel so it knows it is virtualised and asks the hypervisor for help through hypercalls, instead of executing sensitive instructions and being trapped or translated.
example: A Xen PV guest batches page-table updates into one hypercall.

definition: A deliberate call from a guest kernel into the hypervisor, the virtual-machine equivalent of a system call.
example: Xen's mmu_update hypercall asks Xen to validate and apply page-table entries.

aliases: front end and back end drivers
definition: Xen's paravirtual device model: a front-end driver in the guest places requests in shared-memory rings, and a back-end driver in a privileged domain performs the real I/O.
In Xen, the special first VM that has access to real hardware drivers and manages the other guests.
A circular buffer in memory that two parties, such as a guest and a host back end, both read and write, so requests and replies pass without copying through the hypervisor.
A guest driver for a device designed for virtual machines, such as virtio, rather than for real hardware. It talks to the hypervisor directly and avoids slow register-by-register emulation.
A clock source a hypervisor shares with the guest through memory, so the guest can read accurate time without trapping on timer hardware.

A spinlock is a lock a waiting thread busy-waits on. The paravirtual version lets a waiting vCPU tell the hypervisor to run something else, instead of spinning while the lock holder's vCPU is not scheduled.
Hyper-V's channel for paravirtual devices: shared-memory rings and signalling between guests and the host partition.
Intel's hardware support for virtualisation (2005). It adds VMX root mode for the hypervisor and non-root mode for guests, controlled per vCPU by a VMCS.
AMD's hardware support for virtualisation (2006), also called Secure Virtual Machine (SVM). It plays the same role as Intel VT-x, with a VMCB in place of the VMCS.
Advanced Micro Devices, the second major x86 processor maker after Intel.
CPU time a guest's vCPU wanted to run but the host gave to something else. Tools such as top report it as st; a high value means host-side contention.
example: top showing 30% st means a runnable vCPU waited for real CPU almost a third of the time.

definition: Promising guests more vCPUs or memory in total than the host physically has, betting that they will not all use it at once.
A workload sharing a host that uses so much CPU, memory, disk or network that other tenants' performance suffers.
A restricted environment for running code you do not trust, limiting what it can see and touch on the host.
example: gVisor and microVMs are sandboxes for untrusted container workloads.

definition: An Amazon EC2 server rented whole, with no hypervisor between the customer's operating system and the hardware. EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is AWS's virtual-server service.
Microsoft's desktop operating system released in 2001. Xen's 2003 paper described an incomplete port of it to the Xen paravirtual interface.
IBM's large, highly reliable business computers. IBM's 1960s and 1970s systems (CP-40, CP-67, VM/370) pioneered trap-and-emulate virtual machines.
A fatal error from which the kernel cannot recover safely, so it stops the whole operating system.
Moving data between the computer and devices such as disks and network cards. In VMs, I/O is often the costliest part because devices must be emulated or shared.

The two CPU modes added by Intel VT-x (Virtual Machine Extensions, VMX). The hypervisor runs in root operation; guests run in non-root operation, which has its own full set of rings 0–3, so a guest kernel can really run in ring 0.
The CPU switching from the hypervisor into a guest: it loads guest state from the VMCS or VMCB and starts running guest code.

The CPU switching from a guest back to the hypervisor because of an event the hypervisor asked to intercept, such as HLT or an I/O port access. Each exit saves and loads state, so exits are a main cost of virtualisation.
example: A guest NIC driver poking emulated registers may cause several VM exits per packet.

definition: A code the CPU records on a VM exit saying why the guest stopped, so the hypervisor knows what to handle.
example: KVM reports KVM_EXIT_IO when a guest's port I/O needs userspace emulation.

definition: Intel's per-vCPU structure in memory that holds guest state, host state, execution controls and exit information for VT-x.
AMD's per-vCPU control structure for AMD-V, the counterpart of Intel's VMCS, with its own layout.
The part of the VMCS holding the guest's architecturally specified registers (control, segment and execution state), loaded on VM entry and saved on VM exit.
The part of the VMCS describing where and how the hypervisor resumes after a VM exit.
VMCS settings that choose which guest events cause a VM exit, for example HLT, writes to CR3, particular I/O ports or MSRs, or external interrupts.
VMCS fields the CPU fills in on a VM exit, including the exit reason and details of the event.
The x86 instruction that halts the CPU until the next interrupt; an idle kernel runs it. Hypervisors usually exit on it so the idle vCPU's thread can sleep.
The x86 control register that holds the physical address of the top-level page table for the current address space. Writing it switches address spaces.
A separate x86 address space of numbered device registers, read and written with the IN and OUT instructions. Port 0x60 is the classic keyboard controller.
An x86 control register read or written with special instructions (RDMSR, WRMSR), used for CPU features, timers and power settings.
A signal from a device or timer, rather than from the running code, telling the CPU to stop and run a handler. Hypervisors inject virtual interrupts into guests.
The instructions a hypervisor uses to enter a guest: VMLAUNCH (first entry) and VMRESUME on Intel, VMRUN on AMD.
A Linux system call for device-specific commands on an open file descriptor. KVM's whole API is ioctls on /dev/kvm and its VM and vCPU descriptors.
The KVM ioctl that runs a vCPU until something needs userspace. It returns with an exit reason such as KVM_EXIT_IO (port I/O), KVM_EXIT_MMIO (memory-mapped I/O) or KVM_EXIT_HLT.
The variable a C library sets to a numbered error code when a system call fails, such as EINTR, EPERM or ENOMEM.
The error code meaning a blocking system call was interrupted by a signal before it finished. The usual response is to retry.
Device registers that appear at memory addresses, so the CPU talks to the device with ordinary loads and stores. Emulated MMIO accesses cause VM exits.

Page tables a hypervisor builds that map guest virtual addresses straight to host physical addresses, kept in sync with the guest's own tables by trapping its page-table writes. Used before nested paging hardware.
An address used by a program inside a guest. The guest's own page tables translate it to a guest physical address.
What a guest believes is a physical memory address. The hypervisor, or nested page tables, translate it to a real host physical address.
A real address in the machine's RAM.
The CPU hardware that translates virtual addresses to physical ones by walking page tables, caching results in the TLB.
Marking memory pages read-only so that any write traps. Hypervisors use it to notice guest page-table edits and to track dirty pages.

Hardware that adds a second level of translation in the MMU: guest page tables map guest virtual to guest physical, and hypervisor-owned nested tables map guest physical to host physical. Intel calls it EPT; AMD calls it NPT or RVI.
Intel's nested paging (2008, Nehalem): hypervisor-owned tables the MMU walks to translate guest physical addresses to host physical ones.
AMD's nested paging (2007, Barcelona processors), also marketed as Rapid Virtualization Indexing. The equivalent of Intel EPT.
Intel's 2008 processor microarchitecture (first Core i7), which introduced EPT.
A VM exit caused when a guest access is not allowed by the EPT tables, because a mapping is missing or its read/write/execute permissions forbid it.
Recording which guest memory pages have been written since a point in time, using write protection or hardware dirty bits. Live migration relies on it.
A memory page written since it was last copied or saved. During live migration, each round must copy the pages dirtied during the previous round.
Bits in a page-table entry that the MMU sets when the page is read (accessed) or written (dirty), so the OS can tell which pages are in use or modified.
A memory access whose translation is not in the TLB, so the MMU must walk the page tables. Under nested paging this walk can take up to 24 memory reads instead of 4.
The MMU reading page-table entries level by level to translate an address. Page-walk caches keep upper-level entries to shorten it.
One record in a page table, giving the physical page an address maps to plus permission and status bits.
A page table split into a tree of smaller tables. x86-64 uses four levels (five with five-level paging), so a walk reads one entry per level.
A memory page much larger than the normal 4 KiB, typically 2 MiB or 1 GiB on x86-64. One TLB entry then covers far more memory and page walks are shorter.
example: A 2 MiB page covers 512 times the memory of a 4 KiB page.

definition: An Intel feature that tags TLB entries with the guest they belong to, so the TLB need not be flushed on every VM entry and exit.
A tag on TLB entries naming the address space (or, on AMD-V, the guest) they belong to, avoiding flushes on switches. AMD's counterpart to VPID.
A widely supported Intel gigabit network card that QEMU can emulate, so almost any guest has a working driver for it, at the cost of emulation overhead.

A standard family of paravirtual devices (network, block, console and more) designed for VMs. Guest and host exchange buffers through shared-memory virtqueues instead of emulated registers. Now an OASIS standard.
The virtio network device. The guest driver passes packet buffers to a host back end (QEMU, vhost-net or vhost-user) through virtqueues.
The virtio block-storage (disk) device.
A virtio socket device for communication between a guest and its host without a network, addressed by context ID and port.
virtio's shared-memory queue. The driver puts buffer descriptors in a descriptor table and their indexes in the available (avail) ring; the device returns finished ones through the used ring.
A guest's notification to the device that new buffers are waiting. Either side can suppress notifications while busy, so one kick can cover a batch.
A Linux kernel module that handles the virtio-net back end inside the host kernel, so packets need not pass through the QEMU process.
A protocol that hands a virtio back end to a separate userspace process, such as a DPDK virtual switch.
Libraries for very fast packet processing in userspace, polling network cards directly instead of using the kernel network stack.
A non-profit standards body (Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards) that publishes the virtio specification.
Giving a guest direct access to a real hardware device or function, so its driver programs the hardware itself. Fast, but the IOMMU must confine the device's DMA.
A Linux framework (Virtual Function I/O) that safely exposes a PCI device to userspace or a VM, using the IOMMU to restrict the device's DMA.
An MMU for devices: it translates and restricts the addresses a device uses for DMA, so an assigned device can only reach its guest's memory.
The smallest set of devices the IOMMU can isolate from each other. All devices in a group must be assigned together.
An IOMMU feature that checks and redirects device interrupts, so an assigned device cannot fake interrupts to the host or other guests.
Intel's IOMMU technology (Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O).
AMD's IOMMU technology.
The standard bus that connects devices such as network cards and GPUs to the CPU. A PCI function is one logical device on it.
A device reading or writing RAM directly, without the CPU copying each byte. Without an IOMMU, a device can DMA anywhere in memory.
A PCI Express standard that lets one physical device present itself as one physical function plus many lightweight virtual functions, each assignable to a different VM.
example: A 25 Gbit/s NIC can expose dozens of VFs, one per VM.

definition: In SR-IOV, the full-featured PCI function of a device, managed by the host, which creates and configures the virtual functions.
In SR-IOV, a lightweight PCI function with its own queues, created by the physical function and passed to a guest.
The hardware that connects a computer to a network.
AWS's virtualisation architecture, which moves networking, storage and management onto dedicated hardware cards and uses a lightweight KVM-based hypervisor.
Amazon's cloud-computing platform.
Moving a running VM from one host to another with only a brief pause, by copying its memory, CPU and device state while it keeps running.
Live migration that copies all memory while the VM runs, then repeatedly recopies pages dirtied meanwhile, and finally pauses the VM briefly to copy the rest.
Live migration that moves CPU state first, starts the VM on the destination, and fetches memory pages from the source as the guest faults on them.
A QEMU live-migration option that throttles the guest's vCPUs so it dirties memory more slowly and pre-copy can finish.
The final phase of live migration, or a whole migration strategy, in which the VM is paused while remaining state is copied.
The time a migrating VM is paused and not running anywhere, during the final copy and switchover.
An unrequested ARP announcement a machine sends to tell the network which MAC address now owns an IP address. After migration it redirects traffic to the new host.
The USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation, a major systems research conference.
Removing a device from a running system without shutting it down. A VM's SR-IOV VF is often hot-unplugged before migration.
Switching automatically to a backup component when the main one is unavailable, for example from an SR-IOV VF to a virtio NIC during migration.
Running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine, so guests run inside a guest. Possible with KVM and some cloud instance types, with extra translation and exit cost.
Hiding CPU features from guests so every host in a cluster advertises the same baseline CPU model, letting VMs migrate to older hosts safely.
A special x86 firmware mode for power management and platform tasks, hidden from the operating system. Unrelated to running guests.
A binary unit of memory: 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 bytes. Kubernetes writes it Mi.
A binary unit of memory: 1024 bytes. Normal x86 pages are 4 KiB.
A binary unit of memory: 1024 MiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes. Kubernetes writes it Gi.
A decimal unit of data: 1,000,000 bytes. Not quite the same as a mebibyte (MiB).
A decimal unit of data: 1,000,000,000 bytes (1000 MB).
A unit of data, 1000 bytes in decimal use; often loosely used for 1024 bytes, as in '4 KB pages'.
A network speed of 1,000,000,000 bits per second. 10 Gbit/s is at most 1.25 GB/s of data before protocol overhead.
A data rate: gigabytes (or megabytes, MB/s) moved per second.
One thousandth of a second.
example: The default CFS quota period is 100 ms.

definition: One millionth of a second. cgroup cpu.max values are written in microseconds.
RAM the kernel uses to keep recently read or written file data. Clean page cache can be dropped when memory is needed; in cgroups it counts towards a container's memory use.
A Linux kernel feature that wraps a global resource, such as process IDs, mounts or the network stack, so processes inside see their own isolated copy. Linux has eight kinds; containers combine them.
A namespace giving its processes a private copy of the mount table, so mounts made inside need not appear on the host. The first namespace type, added in Linux 2.4.19 (2002).
A namespace isolating the hostname and NIS domain name. UTS stands for UNIX Time-sharing System, after the uname structure that holds them.
A namespace isolating System V IPC objects (shared memory, semaphores, message queues) and POSIX message queues.
A namespace with its own process numbering. Its first process is PID 1 inside it, while having an ordinary PID on the host; a process has one PID per namespace level it is visible in.
A namespace with its own network stack: interfaces, routing table, firewall rules and port numbers. A new one starts with only a loopback interface that is down.
A namespace that maps user and group IDs inside to different IDs outside, and scopes capabilities to resources it owns. UID 0 inside can be an unprivileged UID such as 100000 on the host.
A namespace that hides the host's cgroup paths, so a container sees its own cgroup as the root /.
A namespace (Linux 5.6) letting processes see different monotonic and boot-time clock offsets, mainly so checkpointed containers can be restored elsewhere.
A Linux kernel feature that puts processes into a tree of groups and limits and accounts the CPU, memory, I/O and process count each group uses.
The current cgroup design: one unified hierarchy for all controllers, normally mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup, controlled by files such as cpu.max and memory.max.
The original cgroup design, with a separate tree per controller (for example /sys/fs/cgroup/memory and /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu). Still found on older hosts.
The part of the kernel that enforces one resource type (cpu, memory, io, pids) for cgroups. Domain controllers manage whole processes; threaded controllers can split threads.
A part of the cgroup v2 tree in which threads of one process may be placed in different cgroups, for controllers that support it. It has exceptions to the no-internal-processes rule.
Cgroup v2 rule: a non-root cgroup that distributes domain resources to child cgroups may not contain processes itself. The root cgroup and threaded subtrees are exceptions.
The file system mounted at /. A container gets the image's root file system (its /bin, /lib, /etc) instead of the host's.
A Linux system call that makes a new directory the root mount of the current mount namespace and moves the old root underneath it, so the old root can then be unmounted.
A system call that changes the directory a single process treats as /. It does not change the mount table and is not a security boundary on its own.
The pivot_root argument naming the directory, under the new root, where the old root mount is moved.
An umount2 flag that detaches a mount from the tree immediately but frees it only when nothing still uses it.
A Linux union file system that stacks one or more read-only lower directories under a writable upper directory and shows them as one merged tree. Container runtimes use it for image layers.
A file system built from stacked layers, where upper layers add, change or hide files from lower ones. Lets many containers share one copy of an image.
In overlayfs, the read-only lower layer directories, listed with the top layer first. Several containers can share them.
In overlayfs, the writable upper directory where a container's new and changed files go.
In overlayfs, an empty scratch directory on the same file system as upperdir, used to prepare files before moving them into place atomically. (In a Dockerfile, WORKDIR is unrelated.)
The unified view overlayfs presents: upper files on top of lower ones. It becomes the container's root.
What overlayfs does the first time a lower-layer file is modified: it copies the whole file into the upper layer, then changes the copy.
example: Appending 10 bytes to a 1 GB lower file first copies the full 1 GB into upperdir.

definition: A marker in an upper layer that hides a file from lower layers, used to represent a deletion. overlayfs uses a 0/0 character device or a special xattr; OCI layer tarballs use files named .wh.<name>. The hidden bytes still exist below.
An overlayfs upper directory flagged (with an extended attribute) so nothing from the lower layers' directory of the same name shows through. Used when a deleted directory is recreated.
A name–value pair attached to a file alongside its normal metadata, used by overlayfs, SELinux and others.
A special file representing a device that transfers data as a stream, identified by major and minor numbers. overlayfs uses a 0/0 character device as a whiteout.
A file whose unwritten regions take no disk space. Copying it naively can turn holes into real blocks.
A copy that initially shares the original file's disk blocks and only allocates new ones when either copy changes. Supported by file systems such as XFS and Btrfs.
A contiguous run of disk blocks belonging to a file, recorded as one entry instead of block by block.
Storage managed by Docker (or Kubernetes) that lives outside a container's writable layer, so data persists and avoids copy-up costs.
Mounting an existing directory or file at a second place in the tree, so both paths show the same data.
The list of file systems mounted and where, which a mount namespace keeps private.
A directory where a file system is attached into the tree.
Rules deciding whether a mount made in one mount namespace or place also appears in others (shared, private, slave). Containers normally use private propagation.
A virtual file system at /proc showing kernel information about processes. A container mounts a fresh one so ps sees only its own PID namespace.
The Linux system call that creates a new process or thread. Flags such as CLONE_NEWPID or CLONE_NEWNET put the child in new namespaces.
A system call, and a command that wraps it, that moves the caller into new namespaces (for PID and time namespaces, only its future children).
example: sudo unshare --uts --pid --fork --mount-proc bash starts a shell that is PID 1 with its own hostname.

definition: A system call that joins an existing namespace through a file descriptor such as /proc/<pid>/ns/net. Runtimes use it for docker exec and for joining a pod's shared namespaces.
The Unix system call that creates a child process as a copy of its parent.
The system call that replaces the current process's program with a new one, keeping the same PID.
The system call returning the calling process's PID as seen from its own PID namespace.
The number the kernel uses to identify a process. Each PID namespace has its own numbering.

The first process in a PID namespace. It adopts orphaned processes and must reap them; signals from inside its namespace reach it only if it has installed a handler; and when it exits the kernel kills everything else in the namespace.
Collecting a finished child's exit status with wait(), which removes it from the process table. Unreaped children remain zombies.
A process that has exited but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status, so it still holds a process-table slot.
A process whose parent has exited. It is adopted by the nearest subreaper or by PID 1 of its namespace.
A process marked with prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) that adopts orphaned descendants instead of PID 1.
Signal 15, the polite request to terminate. A process can catch it to clean up; container stop sends it first.
Signal 9, which kills a process immediately; it cannot be caught or ignored. The OOM killer sends it.
A signal that pauses a process; it cannot be caught or ignored.
The signal sent for a bad system call; seccomp's KILL and TRAP actions use it.
A function a process registers to run when a particular signal arrives.
The time a process is given after SIGTERM to shut down cleanly before SIGKILL is sent. Docker's default stop timeout on Linux is 10 seconds.
A virtual Ethernet cable: two linked network interfaces where packets sent into one come out of the other. One end goes in the container's network namespace, the other stays on the host.
A virtual switch in the host kernel that connects several interfaces, such as the host ends of containers' veth pairs.
A virtual network interface (lo, addresses such as 127.0.0.1, named localhost) that delivers packets back to the same network stack. Containers in one network namespace share it.
A 16-bit number identifying a service on a host's network stack. Each network namespace has its own port space.
The number Linux uses to identify a user. UID 0 is root.
The number Linux uses to identify a group of users.
The all-powerful account, UID 0. Linux splits its power into capabilities; in a user namespace container root can be an ordinary user on the host.
Running containers and their runtime without host root privileges, using user namespaces so container root maps to an ordinary host user.
Running the container daemon or runtime as host root, the traditional Docker setup.
The name a machine calls itself. The UTS namespace lets each container have its own.
The domain name used by Network Information Service, an old Unix directory service; isolated with the hostname by the UTS namespace.
The older Unix inter-process communication APIs: shared memory segments, semaphore sets and message queues.
Ways for processes to exchange data or synchronise, such as pipes, sockets, shared memory and message queues.
The IEEE family of standards defining a portable Unix-like operating-system interface. POSIX message queues are one IPC mechanism it defines.
Saving a running process's complete state to disk and recreating it later, possibly on another machine. CRIU does this on Linux.
A clock that only moves forward from an arbitrary start, unaffected by wall-clock changes. The boot-time clock also counts time suspended.
The cgroup v2 file holding a CPU quota and period in microseconds. '50000 100000' allows 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms; 'max 100000' means no limit.
The cgroup v2 file giving a group's relative CPU share under contention, from 1 to 10,000 (default 100).
The cgroup v1 relative CPU share, set in the cpu.shares file (default 1024). Kubernetes counts 1024 shares per CPU of request, then converts shares to cpu.weight on cgroup v2.
The cgroup v2 hard memory limit. Above it the kernel reclaims memory and, if that fails, the cgroup OOM killer acts.
The cgroup v2 memory throttling threshold: above it the group's allocations are slowed and reclaimed, but nothing is killed.
cgroup v2 memory protections: memory below memory.min is never reclaimed, and below memory.low only reclaimed if nothing else is available.
The cgroup v2 file showing the memory currently charged to the group, including page cache.
The cgroup v2 file breaking memory use into anonymous memory, file cache, kernel memory and more.
The cgroup v2 file counting memory events such as hitting high or max, and oom_kill (processes killed by the OOM killer).
The cgroup v2 limit on the number of tasks (processes and threads) in a group. Once reached, fork and clone fail with EAGAIN.
The cgroup v2 file setting per-device read/write bandwidth and IOPS limits.
The cgroup v2 file listing a group's processes; writing a PID to it moves that process into the group.
The cgroup v2 file that enables controllers such as cpu and memory for a group's children.
The cgroup v2 file with CPU statistics, including nr_throttled (periods in which the group was throttled) and throttled_usec (total throttled time in µs).
Input/output operations per second, a measure of storage speed in operations rather than bytes.
A program that creates processes endlessly until the process table or memory is exhausted. pids.max stops it.
The kernel component that, when memory runs out and reclaim fails, chooses a process and kills it with SIGKILL. A cgroup OOM killer picks a victim within the over-limit cgroup.
Running out of memory: no free or reclaimable memory is left for an allocation.
The kernel freeing memory by dropping clean page cache, writing dirty pages back or swapping, before resorting to the OOM killer.
Memory not backed by a file, such as a program's heap and stack. Without swap it cannot be reclaimed.

Linux's long-standing default scheduler for normal tasks, which shares CPU in proportion to weight. Its bandwidth control enforces cgroup CPU quotas. Newer kernels replace it with EEVDF but keep the same quota mechanism.
The CPU time a cgroup's threads may use in total per period, enforced by CFS bandwidth control. When it runs out, the group is throttled until the next period.
Pausing a cgroup's runnable threads because it has used up its CPU quota for the current period. (Memory throttling through memory.high is different: it slows allocations and forces reclaim.)
example: Four busy threads with a 50 ms quota run 12.5 ms, then are throttled 87.5 ms.

definition: Several workloads wanting the same resource, such as CPU, at the same moment. cpu.weight only matters under contention.
A cgroup v2 setting (cpu.max.burst) letting a group carry unused quota into later periods, up to a limit, to absorb short spikes.
A cgroup controller restricting a group to particular CPUs and memory nodes.
The set of CPUs a thread is allowed to run on.
Real elapsed time as a clock on the wall would measure it, as opposed to CPU time, which adds up time across all CPUs used.
The error code meaning not enough memory was available.
The error code meaning 'try again': for example, fork fails with it when pids.max is reached.
The error code meaning no space is left on the device or file system.
The error code meaning permission denied by file permissions or another access check.
The error code meaning operation not permitted, usually for lack of privilege.

The reference implementation of the OCI runtime spec: a command-line tool that takes a bundle and makes the system calls (clone with namespaces, cgroups, pivot_root, capabilities, seccomp, exec) to start a container.
A terminal device; pts/0 is a pseudo-terminal such as an SSH or terminal-window session.
Secure Shell, the encrypted protocol for logging in to and running commands on remote machines. An SSH agent holds keys for other programs to use without exposing them.
A Linux file system held in memory (and swap). Its pages are charged to the writer's cgroup and cannot be dropped like clean disk cache.
A Linux Foundation project, set up in 2015, that publishes open standards for container images, registries and runtimes so tools from different vendors interoperate.
The OCI standard for how an image is laid out: an optional index, manifests, a config and layer blobs, all addressed by digest.
The OCI standard HTTP API that container registries speak for pushing and pulling images.
The OCI standard for running a container from a bundle: an unpacked root file system plus a config.json describing namespaces, mounts, cgroups and the process.
A packaged, read-only template for a container: file-system layers plus a config of runtime defaults, identified by digest and usually stored in a registry.
example: python:3.12-slim is an image; each container started from it gets its own writable layer on top.

definition: Software that turns an image into running containers. High-level runtimes (containerd, CRI-O) manage images and lifecycles; low-level runtimes (runc, crun, runsc) make the kernel calls.
A server that stores and distributes images, speaking the OCI Distribution API.
example: Docker Hub, Amazon ECR and GitHub's GHCR are registries.

definition: Docker's public container registry, the default for docker pull.
Amazon Elastic Container Registry, AWS's container registry service.
GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io), GitHub's container image registry.
Google Cloud's registry service for container images and other packages.
The file in an OCI bundle describing how to run the container: process, mounts, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and seccomp.
A directory containing a container's rootfs/ and config.json, which an OCI runtime such as runc runs.
Storing and naming data by a hash of its contents, so the name always identifies exactly those bytes and identical data is stored once.
An opaque chunk of bytes stored by its digest, such as an image layer or config.
A tar archive of file-system changes (files added or modified, plus whiteouts) that stacks on the layers beneath it to form an image's root file system.
The JSON document in an image giving runtime defaults (Env, Entrypoint, Cmd, WorkingDir, User, exposed ports), build history and the diff_ids of its layers.
The JSON document listing an image's config digest and each layer's digest, media type and size for one platform.
A JSON document pointing to platform-specific manifests, so one tag such as python:3.12 resolves to the right image for each CPU architecture.
A small record pointing at a blob by media type, digest and size.
A cryptographic hash identifying content, written algorithm:hex, such as sha256:4f1c…. Unlike a tag, a digest always refers to exactly the same bytes.
example: myapp@sha256:4f1c… pins one exact manifest.

definition: A cryptographic hash function producing a 256-bit value; the usual digest algorithm for OCI content.
The digest of an uncompressed layer tar, recorded in the image config; the manifest instead lists compressed layer digests.
A string such as application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar+gzip saying what format a blob is in.
A Unix file format bundling many files and their metadata into one stream; .tar.gz is a tar compressed with gzip.
A widely used compression format; most image layers are gzip-compressed tar archives.
A modern compression format from Meta, faster than gzip at similar ratios; supported for OCI layers.
A human-readable, movable name for an image in a repository, such as myapp:v2.3.1 or myapp:latest. It can be repointed to a different manifest at any time.
An image published for several CPU architectures under one name, through an image index.
Names of the two main 64-bit CPU architectures: amd64 (also called x86-64, used by Intel and AMD) and arm64 (64-bit ARM, used by Graviton and Apple silicon).
Storing identical data only once. Content addressing makes layer deduplication natural.
The popular container platform: a CLI, the dockerd daemon, image building and networking, built on containerd and runc.
The Docker daemon. It serves the Docker API on /var/run/docker.sock, builds images and manages networks and volumes, delegating containers to containerd.
A program you drive by typing commands. The docker CLI sends each command as an API request to dockerd.

The Docker command that starts an extra process inside an already running container. The runtime joins that process to the container's namespaces and cgroup (with setns), rather than creating a new container.
example: docker exec -it web sh opens a shell inside the running container named web.

definition: A long-running container daemon that pulls and stores images, prepares snapshots and bundles, and manages container lifecycles through shims. Used by Docker and directly by Kubernetes through its CRI plugin.
A small process that sits between containerd and running containers: it calls runc, keeps container I/O and exit status, and lets containers survive a containerd restart.
The containerd component that unpacks layers and prepares container root file systems, overlayfs by default.
A saved state at a point in time: of a VM's disk and memory, or, in containerd, of a prepared layer stack.
A Docker daemon option that keeps containers running while dockerd is stopped or upgraded.
The gRPC API the kubelet uses to ask a container runtime to run pod sandboxes and containers, pull images and exec commands.
A lightweight container runtime built only to implement the Kubernetes CRI, using OCI runtimes such as runc or crun.
The adapter that let the kubelet use Docker Engine as a runtime; removed in Kubernetes 1.24 (2022).
The Kubernetes agent on every node. It watches pods assigned to its node and drives the container runtime over CRI to run them, and handles eviction.
An open-source system that schedules and manages containers across a cluster of machines (nodes), grouping them into pods.
An OCI runtime written in C, an alternative to runc.
gVisor's OCI runtime: it runs containers inside the gVisor user-space kernel instead of directly on the host kernel.
A text recipe for building an image, one instruction per line (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD and so on).
The Dockerfile instruction that runs a command during the build and saves its file-system changes as a new layer.
The Dockerfile instruction that copies files from the build context (or another stage) into the image, creating a layer.
Like COPY, but can also fetch URLs and auto-extract local tar archives.
The Dockerfile instruction that sets environment variables in the image config; it adds no file layer.
The Dockerfile instruction setting the default command (or default arguments to ENTRYPOINT) recorded in the image config.
The Dockerfile instruction setting the executable a container always runs; CMD supplies its default arguments.
The Dockerfile instruction documenting which ports the container listens on; it only changes metadata.
Dockerfile instructions that pick the base image (FROM), set the working directory (WORKDIR), set the user the process runs as (USER) and add metadata labels (LABEL).
Docker's build engine (the default for Linux images since Docker Engine 23.0). It caches steps by their inputs, builds independent stages in parallel and supports cache and secret mounts.
Saved results of earlier build steps. A step whose inputs are unchanged is reused instead of run again; a changed input invalidates it and the steps that depend on it.
A file listing paths to leave out of the build context sent to the builder, such as .git and node_modules.
The set of files sent to the builder that COPY and ADD can read, usually the directory given to docker build.
Debian and Ubuntu's package manager command. apt-get update refreshes the package lists; apt-get install installs packages.
Python's package installer; pip install -r requirements.txt installs the listed dependencies.
The Git command that downloads a copy of a repository.
A command-line tool for transferring data from URLs.
A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where later stages copy only the outputs they need from earlier ones, keeping compilers and sources out of the final image.
The image a Dockerfile starts FROM, whose layers sit beneath everything the build adds.
Google's minimal base images containing just an application's runtime files, with no shell or package manager.
A compiled language from Google, popular for infrastructure tools (Docker, Kubernetes, gVisor). Go programs are often single static binaries.
Go's mechanism for calling C code. CGO_ENABLED=0 builds without it, usually giving a static binary with no C library dependency.
The compilers, linkers and build tools needed to turn source code into a program.
A compiled program file the operating system can execute. A setuid binary runs with its owner's privileges, not the caller's.
BuildKit mounts that expose a file to a single RUN step only: a cache mount keeps a package cache between builds, and a secret mount provides credentials, without either being saved in a layer.
Merging an image's layers into one so deleted files disappear from the final image. Earlier layers can still remain in caches and history.
AWS's own arm64 server processors.
Apple's arm64 processors (M-series) used in Macs since 2020.
The Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) where dockerd listens. Anyone who can talk to a rootful daemon through it can effectively become root on the host.
Command-line tools for inspecting containers through CRI (crictl) or containerd directly (ctr), the replacements for docker ps on Kubernetes nodes.
The secret half of an SSH key pair, often stored as ~/.ssh/id_rsa. Anyone with it can authenticate as its owner.
Replacing a credential with a new one and revoking the old, done whenever the old one may have leaked.
The Docker command that exports an image, with all its layers, to a tar archive.
All the code and interfaces an attacker can reach and try to exploit. For a native container it includes every system call the host kernel accepts from it.
Using several independent security layers so one failure does not expose everything.
A description of who might attack a system, what they want and what they can do, used to choose defences.
Running workloads from different, possibly mutually hostile, customers (tenants) on shared infrastructure.

Linux's split of root's power into separate privileges, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE or CAP_SYS_ADMIN: 41 of them, numbered 0 to 40, on kernels since 5.9. The kernel checks the relevant capability, not UID 0, before a privileged action.

Each thread has five capability sets: effective (what the kernel checks now), permitted (the most it can make effective), inheritable and ambient (what can pass across exec) and bounding (a limit on capabilities gained from files on exec).
The capability to bind a socket to a privileged port, one below the network namespace's ip_unprivileged_port_start (1024 by default).
The capability to configure networking: interfaces, routes, firewall (iptables) rules and more.
The capability to use raw and packet sockets, as packet sniffers and traditional ping implementations do.
The capability to trace and inspect other processes with ptrace.
The capability to load and unload kernel modules.

A very broad capability covering mounts, namespace operations and many other administrative actions. Often called 'the new root' because granting it gives away most of what capabilities protect. Capability number 21.
The capability to bypass file read, write and execute permission checks.
The capability to use chroot.
The capability to change any file's owner and group. Capability number 0.
Capabilities to change a process's user and group IDs.
The line in /proc/<pid>/status showing a thread's effective capabilities as a hexadecimal bitmask.
example: CapEff: 00000000a80425fb decodes to Docker's 14 default capabilities.

definition: A number whose individual bits are used as yes/no flags, bit c meaning item c.
Base-16 notation using digits 0–9 and a–f; each hex digit is 4 bits. Often written with a 0x prefix.
A bitwise operation giving 1 where two bits differ and 0 where they match; XOR-ing two masks shows which bits changed.
The open-source project underlying Docker Engine; its default capability list and seccomp profile are Docker's defaults.
Removing every capability from a container, then adding back only the few it really needs.
A port below ip_unprivileged_port_start (1024 by default) that only processes with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE may bind. Some runtimes lower the threshold.
The traditional Linux tool for configuring packet-filtering and NAT rules in the kernel.
A system call letting one process observe and control another, used by debuggers and strace.
Either the system call that changes a process's user ID, or the file permission bit that makes a program run as its owner (often root) whoever starts it.
example: sudo is a setuid-root binary.

definition: A setuid-root program that lets permitted users run commands as root.
A per-process flag, set with prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS), after which exec can never grant more privileges (setuid bits and file capabilities are ignored). It is inherited and permanent.
A Linux system call for setting process attributes such as no_new_privs or the child subreaper flag.
A Kubernetes securityContext field; setting it to false makes the runtime set no_new_privs on the container process.

A Linux feature that filters a process's system calls. In filter mode (seccomp-bpf) a small BPF program checks each call's number, architecture and raw arguments and returns an action such as allow or fail.
A small in-kernel virtual machine language originally for filtering packets. seccomp uses classic BPF programs; modern eBPF is a larger extension.
The value a seccomp filter returns for a system call: ALLOW it, fail it with an ERRNO, KILL_PROCESS, TRAP (send SIGSYS to a handler), USER_NOTIF (ask a supervisor process) or LOG and allow.
The integer that identifies which system call a program is making. Numbers differ between ABIs: execve is 59 on x86-64 but 11 on i386.
A C library that builds seccomp filters from readable rules and handles architecture differences.
A policy that allows everything except named items. Weaker than an allowlist, because anything forgotten is allowed.
A policy that denies everything except named items. Docker's default seccomp profile is an allowlist.
A race where something is checked, then changed by another thread or process before it is used, so the check no longer holds.
The kernel framework for mandatory access control modules such as AppArmor and SELinux, which add checks on files, sockets, mounts and other objects.
The machine-level contract between programs and the kernel or libraries: register use, data layout and system call numbers.

The 32-bit x86 system-call interface (named after Intel's 80386). On x86-64 kernels with compatibility enabled, 32-bit code can make i386 system calls through int 0x80, with different syscall numbers from x86-64.
A Linux ABI using 64-bit registers with 32-bit pointers. Its syscalls report AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64 and set __X32_SYSCALL_BIT, so seccomp filters must check for it separately.
The architecture identifier seccomp filters see (for example AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64), used to tell ABIs apart before trusting a syscall number.
A seccomp flag that applies a new filter to all threads of the process at once, instead of only the calling thread.
A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. System call arguments are passed in registers.
A value holding a memory address. seccomp filters see a pointer's number but cannot follow it to the data.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public catalogue of security flaws, each with an ID such as CVE-2022-0847.
A 2022 Linux heap overflow in filesystem-context handling that unprivileged users could reach through user namespaces to gain root; seccomp profiles blocking unshare stopped that route.
A 2022 Linux kernel flaw letting a process overwrite page-cache data of files it could only read, using pipes and splice, on vulnerable kernels.
A 2019 runc vulnerability where a malicious container could overwrite the host runc binary through /proc/self/exe during docker exec, gaining host code execution.
A Linux system call that moves data between a file and a pipe without copying through userspace.
Code that abuses a kernel bug to gain privileges or break out of an isolation boundary such as a container or VM.
Rarely needed Linux system calls: keyctl manages the kernel keyring and kexec_load loads a new kernel to boot. Container seccomp profiles block them.
Security policy set by the administrator and enforced by the kernel on every access, which ordinary users and root processes cannot override.
The ordinary Unix permission model, where a file's owner decides who may access it (owner, group, other bits and ACLs).
A list attached to a file naming extra users or groups and their permissions.
The octal read/write/execute bits for owner, group and others; 0640 means owner read-write, group read, others nothing.
The Linux file holding users' password hashes, readable only by root and the shadow group.
A path-based Linux Security Module used by Ubuntu and Debian. Docker loads a docker-default profile that denies writes to most of /proc/sys and /sys, and mounting.
A label-based Linux Security Module, default on Red Hat systems. Containers typically run with the container_t type and MCS categories.
SELinux categories added to labels so two processes with the same type, such as two containers, can still be kept from each other's files.
A daemonless, Docker-compatible container engine from Red Hat, designed to run rootless.
A Kubernetes pod field; false runs the pod in its own user namespace, so container root maps to an unprivileged host UID.
Google's container sandbox: a user-space kernel written in Go that implements the Linux system-call interface, so applications rarely touch the host kernel directly.
gVisor's user-space kernel process, which handles the application's system calls with its own memory management, VFS and network stack.
gVisor's default platform, which intercepts application system calls using seccomp traps.
A separate gVisor process that performs file-system access on the Sentry's behalf.
The kernel layer that gives one file API over many file systems.
A network protocol implementation; netstack is gVisor's own TCP/IP stack written in Go.
Google Cloud's managed Kubernetes. GKE Sandbox runs pods under gVisor.
Cloud services where you supply code or containers and the provider runs and scales them, with no servers for you to manage.
AWS's minimal KVM-based VMM written in Rust, offering a few virtio devices and no BIOS, to start lightweight microVMs quickly. Used for Lambda and Fargate.
A lightweight virtual machine with a minimal device model, quick to start and small in memory, used to give each workload its own guest kernel.
A memory-safe systems programming language, used for Firecracker, crosvm and Cloud Hypervisor.
A simple text terminal over an emulated serial port, used for boot messages and debugging.
The legacy PC keyboard controller chip. Firecracker emulates just enough of it to let the guest reset the VM.
The firmware that initialises a PC and starts the boot loader. Firecracker skips it and loads the guest kernel directly.
Universal Serial Bus, the standard for connecting peripherals.
The Firecracker API action that boots a configured microVM.
The program a Linux kernel starts first as PID 1.
AWS's serverless functions service, which runs each function in Firecracker microVMs.
AWS's serverless container service, which runs containers without the customer managing servers.
Firecracker's companion program that wraps the VMM process in chroot, namespaces, cgroups and dropped privileges before it starts.
An OCI-compatible runtime that runs each pod inside a lightweight VM (QEMU, Cloud Hypervisor or Firecracker), with an agent inside creating the containers.
A container started with --privileged (or privileged: true in Kubernetes): it gets all capabilities and host devices, and default seccomp and LSM confinement are switched off.
The Kubernetes seccomp profile type meaning 'use the container runtime's default profile'. Localhost selects a custom profile file on the node.
A kubelet setting that applies RuntimeDefault seccomp to every pod that does not choose a profile.
Running with no seccomp filter (or no LSM profile). It is still the Kubernetes default for seccomp unless the kubelet's seccompDefault setting is on or the pod chooses a profile.
Mounting a directory or socket from the host into a container (hostPath in Kubernetes). Sensitive paths can hand the container host data or authority.
One run of an automated build-and-test pipeline in continuous integration.

Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit: one or more containers scheduled together on one node, sharing a network namespace (one IP address) and optionally volumes. On Linux it is anchored by a pod sandbox.
A machine, physical or virtual, in a Kubernetes cluster that runs pods under a kubelet.
The control-plane component that picks a node for each new pod, using the pod's resource requests and constraints.
A human-readable data format using indentation, used for Kubernetes object definitions.
The desired-state section of a pod object, listing its containers, images, resources, volumes and security settings.
The environment a runtime creates for a pod before its containers: on a native Linux node, shared namespaces held by a pause process and a pod cgroup; with Kata, a whole VM.

Operations in the Container Runtime Interface: RunPodSandbox creates the pod's sandbox, PullImage fetches an image, CreateContainer and StartContainer run each container, and Exec runs a command in one.
A tiny container whose process just sleeps, holding a pod's shared namespaces open; it may also act as PID 1 and reap zombies.
The standard for plugins that set up a pod's networking: typically a veth pair, the pod IP address and routes.
A popular CNI plugin providing pod networking and network policy.
A CNI plugin built on eBPF for pod networking, security policy and observability.
Amazon EKS's CNI plugin, which gives pods IP addresses from the cloud network (VPC) directly.
The conventional name of the first Ethernet interface; inside a pod it is the pod's end of the veth pair.
The IP address assigned to a pod's network namespace, shared by all its containers.
An entry telling the network stack where to send packets for a destination.
A helper container running beside the main one in a pod, such as a proxy or log shipper, sharing its network namespace.
A service mesh that routes pod traffic through sidecar proxies (or, with Istio CNI, sets interception up outside the pod).
A container in a pod that runs to completion before the app containers start.
A pod field; true puts all its containers in one PID namespace, with the pause container as PID 1.
The Kubernetes command-line tool. kubectl exec runs a command in an existing container; kubectl debug can add a temporary ephemeral container.
A temporary container added to a running pod for debugging.
The init system and service manager on most Linux distributions, which also manages cgroups through slices and scopes.
How the kubelet and runtime create cgroups: through systemd (recommended on systemd hosts) or by writing cgroupfs directly. Both must use the same one.
systemd units grouping processes in the cgroup tree: a slice is an inner node (such as kubepods.slice), a scope wraps externally started processes such as a container.
A thousandth of a CPU in Kubernetes resource units: 1000m = 1 CPU, 250m = a quarter of a CPU.
The amount of CPU or memory a container asks Kubernetes to reserve. The scheduler places pods by requests; a CPU request becomes a relative cpu.weight.
The most CPU or memory a container may use. A CPU limit becomes a cpu.max quota (throttling); a memory limit becomes memory.max (OOM kill).
A node's capacity minus what is reserved for the system and kubelet: the resources pods can request.
The Kubernetes termination reason for a container whose process was killed for exceeding its memory limit, usually with exit code 137.
The number a process returns when it ends; 0 means success. 128 + n means it was killed by signal n, so 137 means SIGKILL.
A Kubernetes volume that starts empty and lives as long as the pod. With medium: Memory it is a tmpfs in RAM, charged to the pod's memory.
Disk space the kernel uses to hold memory pages moved out of RAM, letting anonymous and tmpfs memory be reclaimed.
The kernel's shared-memory page type, used by tmpfs and shared memory; it can only leave RAM by swapping.
A Kubernetes feature (behind a feature gate) that uses cgroup v2 memory.min and memory.high to protect and throttle container memory.
Kubernetes' classification of pods by their requests and limits: Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort. It sets the OOM score adjustment.
The QoS class for pods where every container sets CPU and memory requests equal to their limits. Their oom_score_adj is −997.
The QoS class for pods that set some requests or limits but do not meet the Guaranteed rule.
The QoS class for pods with no CPU or memory requests or limits at all; first to be killed under pressure (oom_score_adj 1000).
A per-process value from −1000 to 1000 that biases the kernel OOM killer's victim choice; higher means more likely to be killed.
The kubelet terminating pods when a node runs low on memory or disk (for example memory.available below 100Mi), ranked by usage over requests and priority.
The kubelet's eviction signal for free node memory; the default hard threshold on Linux is 100Mi.
A number from a PriorityClass saying how important a pod is, used by eviction and preemption.
A control loop, such as a Deployment or ReplicaSet controller, that creates replacement pods to keep the desired number running.
A pod given a system-critical priority class, which gets special OOM and eviction treatment.
The pod or container section that sets user IDs, capabilities, seccomp, privilege escalation and other kernel security options.
securityContext fields: runAsUser sets the UID the process runs as; runAsNonRoot makes the kubelet refuse to start a container that would run as UID 0.
A securityContext field that mounts the container's root file system read-only.
The securityContext field choosing a seccomp profile: RuntimeDefault, Localhost or Unconfined.
The built-in Kubernetes admission controller that checks pods against the Pod Security Standards for the namespace's label, and can reject them.

Three Kubernetes policy levels: privileged (unrestricted), baseline (blocks known privilege escalations such as privileged containers, host namespaces and hostPath) and restricted (hardened: non-root, drop ALL capabilities, no escalation, seccomp).
A named partition of a Kubernetes cluster's objects, used for access control and policy. Unrelated to Linux kernel namespaces.
The Kubernetes control-plane component that serves the API, validates objects and runs admission.
A key–value tag on a Kubernetes object, such as pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted on a namespace.
Pod fields that make the pod share the node's network or PID namespace instead of getting its own. Meant for node agents.
A privileged program run on every node, such as a log collector or CNI daemon, that needs host access.
A Kubernetes object mapping a name to a CRI runtime handler configured on nodes; a pod's runtimeClassName selects it, for example gVisor (runsc) or Kata.
The name of a runtime configuration in containerd or CRI-O (such as runc, runsc or kata) that a RuntimeClass refers to.
Extra CPU and memory a RuntimeClass declares for each pod's sandbox (such as a Kata VM), which the scheduler adds to the pod's requests.
A Kubernetes on/off switch for alpha or beta features.
Networking where a pod or node has both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
A fixed set of worker threads that run queued tasks. Sizing it to the CPU limit avoids bursts that exhaust the quota.
A file or block device holding the full contents of a virtual disk.
A service whose users notice slow individual responses, so occasional long pauses (such as CPU throttling) matter more than average speed.
A Linux tool showing live CPU use, split into user (us), system (sy), I/O wait (wa), steal (st) and more.
